steps.say: Most baby spit ups are simple immaturity that fades before the first birthday. Poor weight gain plus chest infections, wheeze or breathing pauses marks real disease instead.
steps.tx: Most baby spit ups are immaturity, not disease. Transient vomiting from an immature **lower oesophageal sphincter** (loose milk gate) usually resolves between **6 and 12 months** (six and twelve months). Persistent severe reflux instead causes **failure to thrive** (poor weight gain), recurrent bronchitis, asthma like wheeze, apnea and even stridor events, through repeated micro **aspiration** (acid breathed into the lungs). Poor weight plus chest symptoms marks disease, not posseting.

steps.say: Years of acid can scar the gullet narrow and change its lining. Any child with swallowing trouble years into reflux needs a camera test, because scarring announces itself late.
steps.tx: Years of acid reshape the lining itself. Acid burns can **stricture** (narrow) the oesophagus and convert squamous lining to **Barrett oesophagus** (acid changed lining) with columnar metaplasia, needing periodic **surveillance** (planned camera checks) for dysplasia. Any child with dysphagia years into reflux needs scoping, since a stricture announces itself late and cancer, though rare in children, starts here.

vis.alt: Panels showing erosive oesophagitis, Barrett oesophagus, peptic stricture and adenocarcinoma around a central reflux diagram.
vis.caption: Acid injury marches from erosive oesophagitis to Barrett lining, peptic stricture and cancer, which is why new dysphagia needs scoping. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: The swallow X ray shows shape and blockages while the camera shows burns and allergy. Biopsies settle the allergy mimic, which needs diet change rather than acid drugs.
steps.tx: Two tests answer different questions. A **contrast study** (swallow X ray) shows anatomy and mechanical causes like webs and malrotation but lacks specificity for reflux itself, while **endoscopy** (camera test) shows mucosal injury and detects **eosinophilic oesophagitis** (allergy cell inflammation) that mimics reflux. Biopsies settle the mimic, since allergy cells demand diet change and swallowed steroids, not stronger acid drugs.

steps.say: When the story stays unclear, count the acid directly over a full day. The probe tallies every acid episode, and adding a movement sensor catches even non acid reflux that still triggers cough.
steps.tx: When the story stays unclear, measure the acid itself. The **24 hour** (twenty four hour) oesophageal **pH study** (acid counting test) is the **gold standard** (best test), counting acid episodes with total and longest durations. Combined **impedance** (movement sensor) pH adds liquid versus gas detection, catching non acid reflux that still triggers cough and apnoea in infants.

steps.say: A stomach that empties slowly worsens every reflux, so measure its speed with a tracer milk feed. Half the feed should clear within an hour, and pressure testing is seldom needed in children.
steps.tx: Slow stomach emptying worsens every reflux. The **gastric emptying scan** (milk emptying test) uses a **technetium** (tracer) labelled meal and clears about **50 percent** (fifty percent) of the meal by **60 minutes** (sixty minutes) and **80 percent** (eighty percent) by **90 minutes** (ninety minutes). Delayed clearance pushes management toward prokinetics, while **manometry** (pressure test) is rarely used in children.

steps.say: Start with thicker smaller feeds, upright positioning and acid lowering drugs. Reserve surgery for frightening events, failing growth or scarring, since most infants outgrow the loose gate.
steps.tx: Start gentle and escalate only for harm. First **conservative management** (feed and position care) means thickened feeds, smaller volumes and positioning plus **acid suppression** (acid lowering drugs). A **surgical indication** (reason to operate) needs life threatening events, failure to thrive or stricture, since most infants outgrow the loose gate within the first year and never need a wrap.

steps.say: Wraps differ in how far they circle the gullet. The full circle works best but can bloat and stick swallows, while partial wraps trade a little strength for fewer side effects.
steps.tx: Wraps differ in degrees and trade offs. **Nissen fundoplication** (full stomach wrap) is a **360 degree** (three hundred sixty degree) wrap and the gold standard, but risks bloating and dysphagia despite limited hiatal dissection. **Toupet** (back partial wrap) **270** (two hundred seventy) and **Thal** (front partial wrap) **180 degree** (one hundred eighty degree) partial wraps trade some efficacy for fewer side effects, suiting children with weak gullet squeeze.

vis.alt: Illustration of acid reflux through a loose oesophageal sphincter with hiatus hernia, mucosal erosion and Barrett metaplasia.
vis.caption: Loose sphincter with hiatus hernia, erosion and Barrett change: the anatomy a fundoplication wrap corrects. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Keyhole surgery is the standard route, weak squeezers get partial wraps, and a stomach feeding tube often goes in at the same sitting. Preventive wraps in brain injured children stay debated, because aspiration can persist around any wrap.
steps.tx: Route and patient selection finish the plan. **Laparoscopy** (keyhole surgery) is the standard route, poor motility predicts dysphagia after a full wrap so partial wraps suit **oesophageal dysmotility** (weak gullet squeeze), and a **gastrostomy** (stomach feeding tube) is often placed at the same sitting for feeds and venting. Prophylactic wraps in neurologically impaired children stay controversial for weak airway protection, since aspiration can persist around any wrap.
